title: Redundant UPPER() Blocks the Seek
description: Wrapping both sides in UPPER() is redundant under a case-insensitive collation and disables the index; compare the column directly.
narrative:
## Scenario
A login screen looks up a user by email:

```sql
SELECT CustomerId, Email, Name FROM Customers WHERE UPPER(Email) = UPPER('user12345@example.com');
```

The developer wrapped both sides in `UPPER()` "to be safe" about case. On a 200,000-row table this now scans the whole `IX_Customers_Email` index.

## Why it's slow
SQL Server's **default collation is case-INSENSITIVE** (`..._CI_...`). So `UPPER()` is **redundant** — `Email = 'user12345@example.com'` already matches the stored `User12345@Example.com`. Worse, `UPPER(Email)` is a **function on the column**, which makes the predicate **non-sargable**: the index is ordered by `Email`, not by `UPPER(Email)`, so the engine can't seek and must scan every row.

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** on `IX_Customers_Email` reading all 200k rows for a single match.
- A `CONVERT`/`Compute Scalar` applying `UPPER` before the comparison.

## The fix
Drop the function and compare the column directly. The comparison stays case-insensitive because of the collation, and the index **seeks** straight to the row.
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, Email, Name FROM Customers WHERE UPPER(Email) = UPPER('user12345@example.com');
hints: Look at the operator on Customers -- a Scan touches every row. Why can't it seek IX_Customers_Email?
The index is ordered by Email, not by UPPER(Email). A function on the column defeats the seek.
SQL Server's default collation is already case-insensitive, so just write WHERE Email = 'user12345@example.com'.
